The first photograph ever to be taken in Canada. By Hugh Lee Pattinson. Niagara Falls, 1840.

Here is the original version. The posted image has been cleaned up and flipped left to right.

Hugh Lee Pattinson (1796 – 1858) was an English industrial chemist and entrepeneur. Although known in his time for the patent process for refining silver that bears his name, he is best remembered for his daguerreotype photographs taken in 1840. In that year Pattinson travelled to Canada in the hope of setting up a mining business, stopping at Niagara Falls long enough to make this daguerreotype image.

This photo was rediscovered in 2000 sitting in a box at Newcastle University in England where it had been languishing on a shelf in Special Collections since 1926, when it was given to the library by Pattisons' descendants.

Here's a primer on how we are able to determine various sorts of information about these planets - orbital distance, mass, volume, density, etc. The article describes how this experiment was carried out. If you assume the planets have big gassy atmospheres, like mini gas giants, then there would likely be some sort spectroscopically detectable disruption (in other words, the emitted light from our perspective would look different) particularly during a simultaneous transit, but there wasn't. So that helps tell you the planets have compact, or minimal atmospheres.

And these planets are all within the habitable zone. The habitable zone is just the area where it's possible for surface water, which many believe to be necessary for life, to exist. Too far from the parent star - it's frozen. Too close - it's gas. Put all that together and we we have two rocky planets, and perhaps three, with the potential for having surface water and with various other favorable conditions for life.

The news was that the planets are indeed rocky. It's all like trying to chisel out a picture.
